narrative:
The model estimates an 11% chance that you will fail your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this is generally positive, in this case it contributed toward the failing prediction because students with zero failures who still show risk often have other hidden struggles the model picks up. Second, your strong desire to pursue higher education pushed the prediction in the opposite direction, working to support a passing outcome. Third, your family size of three or fewer members also pulled the prediction toward failing. Most students who pass come from larger families (over 65% have more than three members), so growing up in a smaller household appears to make success slightly harder according to the patterns the model has learned.

To improve, focus on building consistent study habits beyond your current two to five hours per week, reduce your six absences (higher than the average of 3.8 among passers), and lean on the extra educational support you already receive. Since you want to continue studying after school, these small changes can turn your modest risk into a much safer path to passing. (218 words)
